title: Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring: Validity, Ecological Usefulness, and Influencing Factors
authors: Haddad M, Stylianides G, Djaoui L, Dellal A, Chamari K
population: Athletes of any gender, age or competition level in studies using the Foster 2001 session-RPE method (English-language searches 2001-2016: SPORTDiscus, PubMed, Google Scholar)
findings: 950 studies cited the Foster et al. 2001 paper that proposed the session-RPE method.
36 studies examined the validity and reliability of the method using the modified CR-10 scale.

These studies confirmed validity, good reliability and internal consistency of session-RPE in several sports and physical activities, in men and women, children, adolescents and adults, across expertise levels.
The method could be used as a stand-alone training-load monitor, though some authors recommend combining it with physiological parameters such as heart rate.
limitations: Narrative literature search with no stated risk-of-bias assessment or pooled effect size in the abstract; validity analysis restricted to English-language studies; the abstract does not give the sport breakdown (so applicability to distance running is not shown) and does not enumerate the RPE-altering factors it discusses.
implications: Treat session-RPE as validated enough to be the default internal-load measure for all users, including those without HR data.
Offer HR-based load alongside sRPE when HR quality is good, in line with the suggestion to combine the two, rather than replacing sRPE.
Show CR-10 anchors in the UI and keep the question wording constant, since RPE can be altered by factors the review lists; the abstract does not enumerate them, so do not hard-code adjustments.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2017, first author Haddad. Abstract read in Europe PMC; all numbers match. Removed the researcher's unsupported limitation that most included studies are team sports (not stated in the abstract).
